# Introduction

In this Final Project, I am going to be using a dataset I found on Basketball Reference: [2025-26 NBA Player Stats: Totals](https://www.basketball-reference.com/leagues/NBA_2026_per_minute.html). The dataset features data from the 2025-2026 NBA season. Note that I am interested in predicting the number of minutes played and, since the website would only allow me to retrieve the top 500 players, I sorted by that variable before exporting the file.

A few notes to make on the data: First, I'm interested in what is more likely to earn a player playing time but I wanted to control for injuries so I created a column in the dataset which calculated my actual response variable: minutes played per game (`MPG`). Next, there were "missing" values in the 3 point percentage column (`3P%`) that reflected players that didn't attempt a 3 point shot (players who attempted at least one, but didn't make any, already had a value of `0` here). I added `0`'s in the places with missing cells, but I plan on using the `3P` column (made 3 point shots per 36 minutes played) so it should not make a difference in my analysis. Finally, I chose to export the data on a per 36 minutes basis, as cumulative total statistics will be heavily influenced by total minutes played.

There are obviously a lot of player statistics that get tracked but I am going to focus on the following predictor variables (again, all measured per 36 minutes played): three point shots made (`3P`), free throws made (`FT`), total rebounds (`TRB`), assists(`AST`), steals (`STL`), blocks (`BLK`), turnovers (`TOV`), personal fouls (`PF`), points (`PTS`), and position (`Pos`). Note that some of these are often combined in the analysis of NBA players (for instance, often a player's assist to turnover ratio or "stocks" [steals+blocks]). I thought combining these might deprive the model of some information (in exchange for having few variables, which I thought would be negligibly helpful), so I left them separate. 

# Reading in data, setting up libraries

Next, I will read in the data set and load the libraries I'll need for the modeling process. 

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# Load packages for data preparation, visualization, and modeling
library(lubridate)
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidymodels)

#Create data tibble

min_played<-read_csv("../2025-26_NBA_Player_Stats_Per_36.csv")

min_played
```

Note that there there was very little pre-processing that needed to be done, and it was accomplished before reading the data in. 

Another important thing to mention is that we're dealing with numeric variables across the board here, with the exception of `Pos`, and all the columns are already formatted properly. 

# Splitting the data

Next up, I'll set a seed (one I'm partial to, $\approx \tau$), and split the data for modeling purposes (a 70/30 split, as requested). I choose to stratify the data by position, as the roles these players take on during the game can vary wildly. 

```{r}
# Set seed for reproducibility
set.seed(6.28)

# Split data into training and test sets
mp_split <- initial_split(
  min_played, 
  prop = 0.7,
 )

# Isolate training and test sets

mp_train <- training(mp_split)
mp_test <- testing(mp_split)

# verify my 70/30 split
nrow(mp_train)/nrow(min_played)
nrow(mp_test)/nrow(min_played)
```
Doesn't get much better! 

# Creating Cross-Validation Folds

Next up is to create five cross-validation (CV) folds. For the models we'll be looking at, we'll fit using four of the folds and evaluate the resulting prediction on the fifth fold (all within the training dataset). These folds will be kept consistent between the models we use for fitting. 

```{r}
# Set seed
set.seed(6.28)

# Create five folds within training set
mp_folds <- vfold_cv(
  mp_train,
  v=5
)
```


# Fitting models

## Regression Tree Explanation

As mentioned above, we'll be using a variety of predictors in our model and we'll be predicting a numeric variable. So, we'll be using a regression tree here. With a regression tree, the predictor space is divided into regions and then, when making predictions, the observation is placed into one of these regions and (typically) the prediction is the average of the observed values in that region. 

To create these regions, every value of the predictor is used as a potential  splitting point and the squared error loss is calculated. Then, the minimum loss is found and the corresponding value for the prediction variable is used as the splitting point. This creates a branching effect (at each node) and then the process can be repeated down each branch, growing the tree. Of course, this process can lead to too many splits (too "large" a tree) and so these trees are often pruned back to avoid overfitting the data. 

### Setting up the Regression Tree

Before moving on, we should set up a recipe that we'll use for the regression tree and random forest models. This will be pretty straightforward since, with these models, we don't need to normalize the variables. We will, though, need the `Pos` variable set up as a dummy variable.  

```{r}
# Create recipe to be used with both models
mp_recipe <- recipe(MPG ~ `3P` + FT + TRB + AST + STL + BLK + TOV + PF+ Pos, data = mp_train)|>
  step_dummy(Pos)
mp_recipe
```


Next up, though, we will need to look at the hyperparameters we'd like to tune: 

```{r}
#Identify hyperparameters
rt_tune_spec <- decision_tree(
  cost_complexity = tune(),
  tree_depth = tune()
) |>
  set_engine("rpart") |>
  set_mode("regression")
```

The next thing we'll need is a `tree_grid` for use in the tuning process. Because I have so many variables, I feel like I need to give the model room to make a lot of adjustments (e.g., fine tune the tree's depth). It feels like this might make the process take longer but, with what feels like a small sample size (`n`=500) and only 5 folds, it seems worth a shot. I reserve the right to set it back to 5, as we did in the homework, in which case you wouldn't be reading this anyway.

```{r}
rt_tree_grid <- grid_regular(cost_complexity(),
                          tree_depth(),
                          levels = 10)
```

With that, we're ready for our workflow and CV resamples: 

```{r}
#set seed for reproducibility
set.seed(6.28)

#Define workflow
rt_wf <- workflow() |>
  add_model(rt_tune_spec)|>
  add_recipe(mp_recipe)
  

#Set up resamples
rt_res <- rt_wf |>
  tune_grid(
    resamples = mp_folds,
    grid = rt_tree_grid
  )

#View results
rt_res
```

Let's see what we have here: 

```{r}
# Collect metrics
rt_res |> collect_metrics()
```

Let's pare this down a bit, to get a sense for how many models are close to the best: 

```{r}
# Show top 5 models, by chosen metric
rt_res |>
  show_best(metric = "rmse")
```

Looks like there's a tie at the top, but let's crown a winner anyway.

```{r}
#Pick the best tree
best_rt <- rt_res |>
  select_best(metric = "rmse")

best_rt
```

Now, to fit the model to the whole training dataset:

```{r}
#create final workflow
final_rt_wf <- rt_wf |>
  finalize_workflow(best_rt)

#Fit final model to training data
final_rt_fit <- final_rt_wf |>
  last_fit(mp_split)

final_rt_fit |> collect_metrics()
```

Nice! We have ourselves a fitted model!
